units.objective: After this, a child in 7-10 can estimate and compare the areas of two regions by counting grid squares in rows, shown by choosing the larger region and the number of squares.
units.why: Two farmers each claim the bigger field. Counting every square one at a time is slow; counting rows of equal squares is quick.
useElsewhere: Math: area as rows times columns (multiplication)
Economics: how many floor tiles or how much paint a room needs

units.objective: After this, a child in 7-10 can find the distance between two places by counting how many scale-bar lengths fit along the route and multiplying, shown by entering the correct distance in whole units.
units.why: The class trip bus leaves at 9. The teacher wants to know how far it is from school to the museum, and the map only shows a little bar marked "10 km".
useElsewhere: Math: equal groups, skip counting, multiplication
Everyday life: how many blocks to the shop at 100 m each

units.objective: After this, a child in 7-10 can work out how many whole hours a trip takes when the bus covers the same distance each hour, shown by choosing the correct arrival time on a clock.

standard.source: Fragment of the standard's opening seen in a published alignment document (https://www.firstinspires.org/hubfs/Education_Resources/standards-alignment/fll-challenge/fll-challenge-alignments-CC-Math.pdf). Full text not fetched from corestandards.org (404 on 2026-11-10). Confidence MEDIUM.

units.why: The bus drives 40 km every hour and the museum is 120 km away. Will you be back before the lunch bell?
useElsewhere: Math: division as sharing 120 into groups of 40
Physics: later, speed = distance divided by time
Everyday life: planning when to leave for a match

units.objective: After this, a child in 7-10 can locate a place by following two compass clues (north, south, east, west) from a landmark already on the map, shown by a pin dropped within the round's tolerance.
units.why: A treasure map says: two steps east of the fountain, then one step north. Where is the treasure?
useElsewhere: Everyday life: giving a friend directions around school
Math: counting equal steps on a grid

units.objective: After this, a child in 10-18 can compare how crowded two regions are by dividing a count of people by an area, shown by choosing the more crowded region and giving the rate.
units.why: Town A has 1,000 people in 2 square km. Town B has 1,000 people in 8 square km. Which town is more crowded, and how do you know?
useElsewhere: Math: rates as division
Economics: price per item, cost per person
Chemistry: concentration as amount per volume (same idea, different setting)

units.objective: After this, a child in 10-18 can convert a length measured on a map to a real distance using a ratio scale such as 1:50 000, shown by entering the correct distance in km.

standard.source: https://www.thecorestandards.org/Math/Content/7/G/ (read live on 2026-11-11: solve problems involving scale drawings, including computing actual lengths from a scale drawing).

units.why: Your hiking map is drawn at 1:50 000, and the trail is 7 cm long on the map. How far is the real walk, and is it a stroll or an all-day climb?
useElsewhere: Math: ratios and proportional reasoning
Physics: scale models and drawings
Economics: unit price (price per kilo scales the same way)

units.objective: After this, a child in 10-18 can solve time = distance / speed for a planned route, including rearranging it to find the speed or the distance, shown by the correct time on a clock and the correct departure time.

standard.source: https://www.thecorestandards.org/Math/Content/6/RP/ (read live on 2026-11-11: solve unit rate problems including those involving unit pricing and constant speed).

units.why: A friend's train arrives at 3:40 pm, and you live 90 km away. If you ride at a steady 15 km/h, how long is the ride, and when must you leave?
useElsewhere: Physics: speed, velocity and motion graphs
Economics: price x quantity, cost of a trip
Environment: fuel used per trip

units.objective: After this, a child in 10-18 can choose between a short slow road and a long fast road by computing both travel times, shown by the correct choice and both times.
units.why: The mountain pass is 60 km, and you ride it at 20 km/h. The valley road is 90 km, and you ride it at 60 km/h. Which road gets you home first?
useElsewhere: Math: comparing two linear rates
Physics: average speed over several legs
Economics: toll roads and fuel costs versus time saved

units.objective: After this, a child in 10-18 can work out the clock-time difference between two places from their positions east or west of each other, shown by the correct local time at the second place.
units.why: Your cousin lives 6 time zones east of you. When it is 8 pm where you are, what time is it where your cousin lives?
useElsewhere: Math: addition and subtraction with a 24-hour cycle
Physics: Earth turns 15 degrees every hour (360 / 24)
Economics: when markets and shops open across the world

units.objective: After this, an adult learner can explain why a flat world map makes regions near the poles look larger than they are, shown by ranking pairs of regions by true area against how big they appear.
units.why: On a common wall map Greenland looks about as large as Africa, which is far bigger. Plan a paint shipment by the picture and you order the wrong amount.
useElsewhere: Math: spheres versus flat sheets
Physics: why the same sunlight spreads over a bigger area near the poles

units.objective: After this, an adult learner can explain why the shortest flight between two far-apart places looks curved on a flat map, shown by comparing a great-circle distance with a straight line drawn on a flat map and choosing the shorter.
units.why: A flight from one continent to another takes a path that bends toward the pole on the wall map. Surely a straight line is shorter?
useElsewhere: Math: geometry on a sphere
Physics: why shortest paths on curved surfaces differ from flat ones
Economics: fuel cost of long-haul routes

units.objective: After this, an adult learner can compare the total cost of two routes by combining distance, fuel use, a fare or toll and time, shown by the correct cheaper option and the cost difference.
units.why: A delivery van can take the toll road or the free road. The toll saves an hour, but is an hour worth the fee and the fuel?
useElsewhere: Economics: break-even and comparing costs
Math: linear models with two variables
Environment: fuel use per route

social-studies:region:area-by-squares.prompt: One field covers 3 rows of 4 grid squares. Another field covers 2 rows of 4 grid squares. Which field is bigger, and by how many squares?
social-studies:region:area-by-squares.derivation: 3 × 4 = 12 squares and 2 × 4 = 8 squares; 12 − 8 = 4, so the first field is bigger by 4 squares.

social-studies:route:count-the-steps.prompt: The map's scale bar is marked 10 km. The route from school to the museum measures 4 bar lengths along the map. How far is the trip?

social-studies:route:trip-clock.prompt: The bus drives 40 km every hour, and the museum is 120 km away. How many hours does the trip take?

social-studies:region:density.prompt: Town A has 1,000 people in 2 square km. Town B has 1,000 people in 8 square km. Which town is more crowded?
social-studies:region:density.derivation: Town A: 1,000 ÷ 2 = 500 people per square km. Town B: 1,000 ÷ 8 = 125 per square km, so Town A is more crowded.

social-studies:route:scale-ratio.prompt: A hiking map is drawn at a scale of 1:50,000. The trail measures 7 cm on the map. How far is the real walk?
social-studies:route:scale-ratio.derivation: 7 × 50,000 = 350,000 cm on the ground, and 350,000 cm = 3.5 km.

social-studies:route:travel-time.prompt: You live 90 km from the station and ride at a steady 15 km/h. How long does the ride take?

social-studies:region:flat-map-area.prompt: On a common flat wall map, Greenland looks about as large as Africa. What is really true?
choices: Africa is far bigger — the flat map stretches places near the poles
Greenland and Africa are the same size
Greenland is really bigger than Africa
social-studies:region:flat-map-area.correct: Africa is far bigger — the flat map stretches places near the poles
social-studies:region:flat-map-area.derivation: A flat map stretches regions near the poles, so Greenland only looks as large as Africa; Africa is far bigger.

social-studies:route:great-circle.prompt: On a flat map, a long flight's shortest path bends toward the pole instead of looking straight. Why?
choices: That curved-looking path is the shortest route on the round Earth
Pilots curve the path to save paperwork
A straight line on the flat map is always shorter
social-studies:route:great-circle.correct: That curved-looking path is the shortest route on the round Earth
social-studies:route:great-circle.derivation: The Earth is round: the shortest surface route follows a great circle, which looks curved on a flat map.

social-studies:place:compass-clue.prompt: A treasure map says: two steps east of the fountain, then one step north. Where is the treasure, compared with the fountain?
social-studies:place:compass-clue.derivation: East moves you to the right on the map and north moves you up, so the steps land north-east of the fountain.

social-studies:route:fastest-or-shortest.prompt: The mountain pass is 60 km, and you ride it at 20 km/h. The valley road is 90 km, and you ride it at 60 km/h. Which road gets you home first?
social-studies:route:fastest-or-shortest.derivation: Pass: 60 ÷ 20 = 3 hours. Valley: 90 ÷ 60 = 1.5 hours, so the longer valley road gets you home first.

social-studies:compare:time-zones.prompt: Your cousin lives 6 time zones east of you. When it is 8 pm where you are, what time is it where your cousin lives?
social-studies:compare:time-zones.derivation: Places east of you are ahead in time: 8 pm + 6 hours = 2 am the next day.

social-studies:compare:trip-cost.prompt: With these example prices, a delivery van can take the toll road: 80 km, $10 of fuel plus a $6 toll. Or the free road: 100 km, $13 of fuel and no toll. Which route costs less money, and by how much?
social-studies:compare:trip-cost.derivation: Toll road: $10 + $6 = $16. Free road: $13. $16 − $13 = $3, so the free road costs $3 less.
